cards.text: We're near the end of a love song, friend, a song full of two lovers praising each other (Song of Solomon 4:1-7; 5:10-16). Now a voice asks who this is, coming up and leaning on her beloved. The only thing I ever leaned on was a pile of takeout menus in a junk drawer.

cards.question: She's coming up, leaning on her beloved. Where is she coming up from?

cards.text: Then a memory of waking someone under the apple tree, the very spot where that one's mother gave birth. My family landmark is the back of a junk drawer, friend, and NOBODY is putting a plaque on that.
Then a big request: "Set me as a seal over your heart, as a seal upon your arm." As a cookie stamper, I have to say it. I RESPECT anybody who wants to leave a mark.

cards.question: The request is to be set as a seal over the heart. What reason does the song give right after it?

answers.text: Love is as strong as death

cards.text: Its jealousy is as unrelenting as Sheol, and its sparks are fiery flames, the fiercest blaze of all. I work next to ovens ALL DAY, friend, and even I'm taking a step back.

cards.question: Love's sparks are the fiercest blaze of all. True or false: the song is saying love burns out fast.
Love burns that hot. So what can mighty waters do to it?

answers.text: They put it out in time

cards.text: Rivers can't sweep it away either, and then the song asks about money: what if a man gave all the wealth of his house for love? Somebody once bought ME for a quarter at a closing sale, so I am VERY invested in this answer.

cards.question: If a man gave all the wealth of his house for love, his offer would be utterly ___.

cards.text: Then the song shifts: "We have a little sister," and she's still young. I raised six little cookie cutters, friend, so a family huddle about the little one? I have BEEN in that huddle.

cards.question: The speakers have a little sister who is still young. What are they wondering about her?

answers.text: What to do for her when she is spoken for
How to keep her at home for good
Who should teach her the old songs

cards.text: Here's the plan: if she is a wall, they'll build a tower of silver on her, and if she is a door, they'll enclose her with panels of cedar. Silver towers, cedar panels. Friend, the fanciest thing anybody ever put around ME was a rubber band.

cards.question: The plan for the little sister has two options, a wall or a door. Then a woman speaks up and says she is a ___.
The woman says she is a wall, all grown up now. So what has she become in his eyes?

answers.text: Like one who is far away

cards.text: Solomon, king of Israel (1 Kings 4:1), had a vineyard in Baal-hamon, and each tenant had to bring a thousand shekels of silver for its fruit. My rent in the junk drawer was free, and friend, I STILL overpaid.

cards.question: Solomon's vineyard is leased out to tenants. But the speaker says their own vineyard is theirs to ___.
True or false: the speaker says the thousand shekels are for Solomon.

cards.text: Two hundred go to those who tend its fruit, and friend, I LOVE a boss who pays the crew. Then a call goes out: "You who dwell in the gardens, my companions are listening for your voice."

cards.question: The companions are listening for the voice of the one in the gardens. True or false: the speaker wants to hear that voice too.

cards.text: And here it is, friend, the very last line of the whole Song of Solomon, and it invites the beloved to come away. No fireworks, no big finale, just an invitation, and believe me, I know what a good invitation can do.

cards.question: The last line invites the beloved to come away. The beloved is asked to be like what on the mountains of spices?

answers.text: A gazelle or a young stag

findings.problem: This story card is 3 sentences: the quote of 8:6a, "As a cookie stamper, I have to say it," and "I RESPECT anybody who wants to leave a mark." Only the opening card can run to 3.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card says "the song asks about money: what if a man gave all the wealth of his house for love?" Song 8:7 doesn't ask anything. It states a condition and its result: "If a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love, his offer would be utterly scorned." Calling it a question changes what the text is.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: This story card is 3 sentences: "Then the song shifts... she's still young," "I raised six little cookie cutters, friend, so a family huddle about the little one?" and "I have BEEN in that huddle."

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This story card is 3 sentences: "Here's the plan: ...panels of cedar," "Silver towers, cedar panels," and "Friend, the fanciest thing anybody ever put around ME was a rubber band."

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The closing line, "No fireworks, no big finale, just an invitation, and believe me, I know what a good invitation can do," is pleasant but not funny. Papa Dorin is supposed to go for a real laugh when the moment can hold one, and this one can.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: The question asks "what has she become in his eyes?" but no card ever says who "he" is. Song 8:10 doesn't name him either.
findings.question: Two rules pull against each other here. The text leaves the man unnamed, and "leave open what the text leaves open" says not to name him. But "always give context in the question" says never to use "him" without saying who. Should the question keep the text's open "his eyes," or reword it to something like "in the eyes of the man she loves"?
